title: Learn by Doing: Arrays
lead: The topic sat as a paper: its objective questions, then every past question that walks an array, each with its model answer, and the four patterns taught from nothing.
intro:
Part A is the objective questions on this topic. Part B is past questions only, and no topic carries more of them: the consecutive duplicates, the discount loop, the temperature streak, the parking batch and countNegatives are all one array walk with a different test inside.

Learn the four patterns as METHODS THAT RETURN, because that is how both papers ask for them.

lockin.big: "Declare, create, fill, walk. length is a field with no brackets, and the last index is length minus 1."
lockin.sub: Four patterns: total, count matching, best so far, and the neighbour comparison a[i] against a[i-1]. Each one is a method that returns a value.

methodFrames.teach:
An array is a fixed length row of values of one type. Three steps: declare, create with a size, then fill.

public class Walk {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] nums = new int[5];        for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) nums[i] = (i + 1) * 10;        int[] given = {4, -2, 7, -9, 3};        System.out.println(nums.length + " " + nums[nums.length - 1]);        try {            System.out.println(given[5]);        } catch (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException e) {            System.out.println("caught: " + e.getMessage());        }    }}
Output5 50
caught: Index 5 out of bounds for length 5
methodFrames.ask: What is the highest index of an array created with new int[5], and what happens if you use 5?

methodFrames.teach:
The highest index is 4, and index 5 throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, which 24/25 asks you to define by name. The loop condition is therefore i < nums.length, never <=.

length is a field on an array, with no brackets, unlike a String's length().
methodFrames.ask: Now the patterns. Write, in your head, a method that returns the total of an array.

methodFrames.check: A running total set to zero before the loop, added to inside it, returned after it.
methodFrames.teach:
Here are the four the exam wants, each as a method that returns, which is exactly how the papers word it.

public class Patterns {    static int total(int[] a) {        int sum = 0;        for (int x : a) sum += x;        return sum;    }    static int countNegatives(int[] a) {        int count = 0;        for (int x : a) if (x < 0) count++;        return count;    }    static int largest(int[] a) {        int best = a[0];        for (int x : a) if (x > best) best = x;        return best;    }    static int consecutiveDuplicates(int[] a) {        int pairs = 0;        for (int i = 1; i < a.length; i++) if (a[i] == a[i - 1]) pairs++;        return pairs;    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] sales = {12, 12, -5, 30, 30, 30, -1};        System.out.println(total(sales));        System.out.println(countNegatives(sales));        System.out.println(largest(sales));        System.out.println(consecutiveDuplicates(sales));    }}
Output108
2
30
3
methodFrames.ask: Read the four and predict the four printed values.

methodFrames.teach:
108, 2, 30, 3. Notice what the fourth one does differently: it starts at i = 1 and looks BACK at a[i - 1]. Every question about repeats, streaks or rises uses that one line.

Notice too that the best so far pattern starts from a[0], not from zero: start from zero and an array of negatives returns the wrong answer.
methodFrames.ask: A streak question asks for the LONGEST run. What two variables does that need?

methodFrames.check: One for the run you are in, one for the longest seen.
methodFrames.teach:
A current run and a best run: extend current when the test holds, reset it to zero or one when it breaks, and update best whenever current beats it. That is the cold storage temperature question in one sentence.

public class Grid {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[][] marks = { {70, 65}, {40, 55}, {90, 80} };        for (int r = 0; r < marks.length; r++) {            int sum = 0;            for (int c = 0; c < marks[r].length; c++) sum += marks[r][c];            System.out.println("row " + r + " total " + sum);        }    }}
Outputrow 0 total 135
row 1 total 95
row 2 total 170
methodFrames.ask: Last: two dimensions. How do you walk a table of rows and columns?

methodFrames.check: Nested loops, the inner one bounded by that row's own length.
methodFrames.teach: A loop inside a loop: the outer over marks.length, the rows, the inner over marks[r].length, that row's columns. Writing the inner bound as marks.length is a planted error, and it only shows when the table is not square.

questions.heading: 2025/2026, Question One, 5 marks

scenario.text:
[5 Marks]C. This code is supposed to: Loop through the array, and for each starting index i, find the first number (from i onward) that's a multiple of 4. Add (that number - 1) to sum, count it as a match, stop after 3 matches, then display the sum and match count. Find the errors if the correct output should be:

Sum: 141.0        Matches: 3

exam.answer:
Q1 c · find the errors · 5 MARKS

Read the output first. "141.0" tells you the sum is a double before you have read a line of code. That single character finds two of the five errors.

Code · the paper's snippet, with every error marked · AS PRINTED
import javax.swing.JOptionPane;public class Snippet {public static void main(String[] args) {int[] arr = {24.0, 40.0, 66.0, 80.0, 98.0};        // ERROR 1 and 2  int sum = 0;                                     // ERROR 2  int matches = 0;  boolean stop = false;  for (int i = 0; i <= arr.length && !stop; i++) {   // ERROR 3      for (int j = i; j < arr.length; j++) {          if (arr[j] % 4 == 0) {                     // ERROR 4              continue;          }          sum += arr[j] - j;                        // ERROR 5          matches++;          if (matches == 3) {              stop = true;          }          break;      }  }  JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(null, "Sum: " + sum);  JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(null, "Matches: " + matches);  System.exit(0);}}
Worked example · The five errors, and why each is one
  1. Line 4: int[] cannot hold 24.0. Those are double literals. This is a compile error: "incompatible types: possible lossy conversion from double to int". Fix: double[] arr. The output confirms it: 141.0 is a double.
  2. Line 5: int sum cannot total doubles, and could never print "141.0". Fix: double sum = 0; Unit 3.3: the type decides what you may do and how it prints.
  3. Line 8: i <= arr.length is off by one. Indexes run 0 to length-1 (F.10). Fix: i < arr.length. Here it would not actually throw, because the inner loop never runs when i = 5, but it is still wrong and it is one of the five marks.
  4. Lines 10 to 12: the continue is inverted. The spec says find numbers that are multiples of 4. This skips them and processes everything else: precisely backwards. Fix: if (arr[j] % 4 != 0) continue; Unit 4.7: read every continue as "unless". This is the error worth the most attention, because it is the one that is pure logic.
  5. Line 13: arr[j] - j subtracts the index. The spec says add (that number - 1). Fix: sum += arr[j] - 1; A subtle one: with j it would give the right answer for j = 1 only, so a spot check could miss it.
Code · corrected, and it reproduces the paper's answer · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
// JOptionPane replaced by println so the output can be printed here;// in the exam, keep the dialogs exactly as the paper has them.public class Q1C {    public static void main(String[] args) {        double[] arr = {24.0, 40.0, 66.0, 80.0, 98.0};   // fix 1        double sum = 0;                                 // fix 2        int matches = 0;        boolean stop = false;        for (int i = 0; i < arr.length && !stop; i++) {  // fix 3            for (int j = i; j < arr.length; j++) {                if (arr[j] % 4 != 0) {                   // fix 4                    continue;                }                sum += arr[j] - 1;                      // fix 5                matches++;                if (matches == 3) {                    stop = true;                }                break;            }        }        System.out.println("Sum: " + sum);        System.out.println("Matches: " + matches);    }}
OutputSum: 141.0
Matches: 3

That is the proof. The paper printed Sum: 141.0 and Matches: 3, and the corrected program produces exactly that. If your five fixes do not reproduce the stated output, one of them is wrong, and the paper has handed you the means to check your own answer.

Note i = 2 skipped 66 and found 80, which is exactly what the inner loop is for: "the first multiple of 4 from i onward". And the outer loop never reached i = 3, because stop ended it.

questions.heading: 2025/2026, Question Two, 5 marks

scenario.text:
[5 marks]C. This code is supposed to loop through an array of prices, skip anything under 20, apply a 10% discount to prices 20 and above, add the discounted price to total, count it, and stop once 4 items have been discounted. Then it displays the total and count. Find the errors if the correct output should be:

Total: 202.725  Count: 4

exam.answer:
Q2 c · find the errors · 5 MARKS

The same five errors as Q1, in the same order. This is the payoff of the template.

Worked example · The five errors
  1. Line 4: int[] prices = {15.5, ...}. Decimal literals in an int array: a compile error. Fix: double[] prices. The output "202.725" says double before you read anything else.
  2. Line 5: int total = 0; cannot hold 202.725. Fix: double total = 0;
  3. Line 8: i <= prices.length is off by one. Fix: i < prices.length. Unlike Q1, this one would throw ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at i = 6, because line 9 reads prices[i] straight away. Same error, worse consequence.
  4. Line 9: if (prices[i] > 20) continue; is inverted. The spec says skip anything under 20. This skips everything over 20, i.e. exactly the items to be discounted. Fix: if (prices[i] < 20) continue;
  5. Line 15: if (count == 5). The spec says stop once 4 have been discounted. Fix: if (count == 4). Only four of the six prices are 20 or above anyway, so with == 5 the flag never fires. The count would still be 4, and the total would still be right, which makes this the easiest error to miss: it does not change the answer, it just means the code does not do what it was asked.
Code · corrected, reproducing the paper's answer · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class Q2C {    public static void main(String[] args) {        double[] prices = {15.5, 42.0, 8.75, 60.0, 33.25, 90.0};  // fix 1        double total = 0;                                        // fix 2        int count = 0;        boolean done = false;        for (int i = 0; i < prices.length && !done; i++) {         // fix 3            if (prices[i] < 20) {                                 // fix 4                continue;            }            double discount = prices[i] * 0.1;            total += prices[i] - discount;            count++;            if (count == 4) {                                     // fix 5                done = true;            }        }        System.out.println("Total: " + total);        System.out.println("Count: " + count);    }}
OutputTotal: 202.725
Count: 4

Matches the paper exactly.

questions.heading: 2025/2026, Question Three, 12 marks

scenario.text:
(12 marks)A. A store records daily sales in an integer array saleAmounts[], in the order the sales happened. A "consecutive duplicate" is any position i (i >= 1) where saleAmounts[i] == saleAmounts[i-1].

Given the array:

Index0123456789
Amount20203540404015606025

Write a program that:

i.    Create a method that makes one pass through the array and returns the count of indices i >= 1 where saleAmounts[i] == saleAmounts[i-1].

ii.   Create a method that returns a single String listing, in original order and comma-separated, every sale amount that equals its predecessor or its successor in the array. Build this string using plain String concatenation only (no StringBuilder, no array of booleans returned). Index 0 checks only its successor; the last index checks only its predecessor.

iii.  Using JOptionPane, display one dialog showing (a) the total consecutive-duplicate count from part 1, and (b) the flagged-amounts string from part 2.

[Hint: To aid your flow trace your algorithm by hand first: it must not flag 35, 15, or 25.]

exam.answer:
Q3 a · consecutive duplicates in a sales log · 12 MARKS
Index0123456789
Amount20203540404015606025

Write a program that (i) counts, in one pass, the indices i >= 1 where the amount equals the one before it; (ii) returns a single String listing, in order and comma separated, every amount that equals its predecessor or its successor, built with plain String concatenation only; (iii) displays both in one JOptionPane dialog. The paper adds a hint: it must not flag 35, 15, or 25.

Must memorise · Parts i and ii count DIFFERENT things

Part i counts positions. Part ii lists values. They are not the same question asked twice, and they do not give the same number.

Part i asks how many boundaries have a twin across them. Part ii asks which elements are touching a twin at all.

Look at the three 40s. They contain two boundaries (index 3 to 4, and 4 to 5) but three elements. So part i counts 2 there and part ii lists 3. Read the two parts as one question and you will answer one of them wrong.

MEMORY HOOK: fences and posts. Part i counts the fences between posts, part ii counts the posts. A run of n twins has n posts and n-1 fences, always.

Dry run · Both answers, by hand, before writing any code

Check it against the hint. The paper told you 35, 15 and 25 must not be flagged, and they are the only three that are not. The examiner has handed you a way to test your own trace before you write a line of code, which is exactly what the hint is for.

And check the two answers against each other. The runs are 20-20 (2 long), 40-40-40 (3 long) and 60-60 (2 long). Part ii flags 2 + 3 + 2 = 7 values. Part i counts 1 + 2 + 1 = 4 positions. They differ by exactly 3, the number of runs, because each run loses one to the fences-and-posts rule. If your two answers do not differ by the number of runs, one of them is wrong.

Code · question three, part a · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class SalesDuplicates {    // Part i: ONE pass. Count every index i >= 1 whose amount equals the one before.    static int countConsecutiveDuplicates(int[] sales) {        int count = 0;        for (int i = 1; i < sales.length; i++) {            if (sales[i] == sales[i - 1]) {                count++;            }        }        return count;    }    // Part ii: every amount equal to its predecessor OR its successor, in order,    // comma separated, built with plain String concatenation only.    static String flaggedAmounts(int[] sales) {        String result = "";        for (int i = 0; i < sales.length; i++) {            boolean sameAsPrevious = (i > 0) && (sales[i] == sales[i - 1]);            boolean sameAsNext = (i < sales.length - 1) && (sales[i] == sales[i + 1]);            if (sameAsPrevious || sameAsNext) {                if (result.equals("")) {                    result = "" + sales[i];                } else {                    result = result + ", " + sales[i];                }            }        }        return result;    }    // Part iii: one dialog showing both answers.    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] saleAmounts = {20, 20, 35, 40, 40, 40, 15, 60, 60, 25};        int duplicates = countConsecutiveDuplicates(saleAmounts);        String flagged = flaggedAmounts(saleAmounts);        String message = "Consecutive duplicate count: " + duplicates                       + "\nFlagged amounts: " + flagged;        System.out.println(message);    }}
OutputConsecutive duplicate count: 4
Flagged amounts: 20, 20, 40, 40, 40, 60, 60

Exactly the hand trace, including the three amounts the paper told us not to flag. The dialog is a println here so its text can be printed in this book; in the hall, write JOptionPane.showMessageDialog(null, message); and import javax.swing.JOptionPane (F.11).

Trap · Three ways to lose marks on part A

1. Starting part i's loop at 0. The question says i >= 1, and for a reason: sales[0 - 1] is sales[-1], which throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException (Unit 8.1). Index 0 has no predecessor, so the loop starts at 1. This is where "one pass" is easiest to get right and easiest to throw away.

2. Forgetting the boundary guards in part ii. Index 0 has no predecessor and the last index has no successor. The guards (i > 0) and (i < sales.length - 1) are what stop the reads from running off either end. They work because && is short-circuit (Unit 3.6): when i > 0 is false, Java never evaluates sales[i - 1], so it never throws. Swap the two sides of the && and the program crashes on the first element.

3. The leading comma. Concatenating ", " + sales[i] every time gives , 20, 20, 40... with a comma stuck on the front. The test if (result.equals("")) writes the first value bare and every later value with its separator in front. Compare Strings with .equals(), never with == (Unit 7.3).

The question bans StringBuilder deliberately: it wants to see that you can handle the separator yourself. Use StringBuilder anyway and you have answered a question the paper did not ask.

questions.heading: 2025/2026, The cold-storage log, 13 marks

scenario.text:
(13 marks)B. A cold-storage warehouse records its internal temperature once every hour, for 24 hours. Write a program, using JOptionPane only for input/output, that checks the day's temperature log for sustained breaches of a safe limit. A reading is a breach if it is above 8°C.

i.    Using a loop, prompt the user 24 times (one dialog per hour) for that hour's temperature. Each input must be validated: it must parse as a number between -20 and 50 inclusive. If invalid, re-prompt for the same hour (using a nested loop/control statement) until a valid value is entered. Store all 24 valid readings in a 1-D array.

ii.   Scan the 24-hour array once to find every maximal run of consecutive breach-hours (temperature > 8°C). Using only loops and conditionals (no extra arrays), determine:

•  the total number of qualifying streaks, where a qualifying streak is any consecutive run of 3 or more breach-hours;

•  the length (in hours) of the single longest breach streak anywhere in the log.

iii.  Using nested if-else logic, classify the day as exactly one of:

•  "CRITICAL": longest streak >= 6 hours

•  "WARNING": longest streak is 3-5 hours (inclusive)

•  "SAFE": no streak of 3 or more consecutive breach-hours occurred

iv.  Show one JOptionPane dialog stating: the total number of qualifying streaks, the longest streak length, and the final classification.

exam.answer:
Q5 b · sustained breaches of a safe limit · 13 MARKS
  1. prompt 24 times, one dialog per hour. Each input must parse as a number between -20 and 50 inclusive; if invalid, re-prompt for the same hour using a nested loop, until valid. Store all 24 in a 1-D array;
  2. scan the array once, using only loops and conditionals (no extra arrays), to find the number of qualifying streaks (runs of 3 or more consecutive breach-hours) and the length of the longest breach streak;
  3. using nested if-else, classify: CRITICAL if the longest streak is >= 6, WARNING if it is 3 to 5, SAFE if no streak of 3 or more occurred;
  4. show one dialog with the streak count, the longest length, and the classification.
Must memorise · Count the run when it turns 3, and measure it as you go

The whole of part 2 is three variables and one pass:

currentRun: breach hours in a row right now, reset to 0 on any non-breach.
longestStreak: updated every breach hour, not at the end of a run.
qualifyingStreaks: incremented when currentRun == 3, exactly.

Why == 3 and not >= 3. A run passes through 3 exactly once, on its third hour. So == 3 counts each qualifying run once, however long it becomes. Use >= 3 and a 6-hour run is counted four times, giving 4 streaks where there is one.

MEMORY HOOK: a run is counted at the moment it qualifies, not while it continues. The threshold is a door you pass through once, not a room you stay in.

Trap · The streak that is still running when the day ends

The instinct is to close each run in the else, where the non-breach hour is: "the run just ended, so now measure it."

if (readings[hour] > 8) {    currentRun++;} else {    if (currentRun > longestStreak) longestStreak = currentRun;  // non-breach only    if (currentRun >= 3) qualifyingStreaks++;    currentRun = 0;}

It works, until the day ends mid-streak. If hours 18 to 23 are all breaches, the loop finishes with currentRun = 6 and never reaches the else. The longest streak of the day is never measured and never counted. The program reports SAFE on a day the freezer was over temperature for six straight hours.

The fix is not to bolt a copy of the else-block on after the loop. That is the usual patch and it duplicates the logic in two places, so the next edit changes one and forgets the other. Instead, update on every breach hour:

Measure longestStreak as the run grows, and count the run the instant it turns 3. Then a run that is still going when the array ends has already been measured and already been counted, and the end of the array needs no special case at all.

This is worth more than one exam question. A boundary you never treat specially cannot be got wrong at the boundary.

Code · question five, part b · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
import java.util.Scanner;public class ColdStorage {    public static void main(String[] args) {        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);        double[] readings = new double[24];        // Part i: 24 prompts, each re-prompted until the value is valid.        for (int hour = 0; hour < 24; hour++) {            boolean valid = false;            while (!valid) {                String typed = in.nextLine();                try {                    double t = Double.parseDouble(typed);                    if (t >= -20 && t <= 50) {                        readings[hour] = t;                        valid = true;                    } else {                        System.out.println("  hour " + hour + ": " + t                            + " is outside -20 to 50. Asking again.");                    }                } catch (NumberFormatException e) {                    System.out.println("  hour " + hour + ": \"" + typed                        + "\" is not a number. Asking again.");                }            }        }        // Part ii: ONE scan, no extra arrays.        int currentRun = 0, longestStreak = 0, qualifyingStreaks = 0;        for (int hour = 0; hour < 24; hour++) {            if (readings[hour] > 8) {                currentRun++;                if (currentRun > longestStreak) {                    longestStreak = currentRun;                }                if (currentRun == 3) {                    qualifyingStreaks++;                }            } else {                currentRun = 0;            }        }        // Part iii: classify. questions.heading: 2025/2026, The parking garage, 13 marks

scenario.text:
(13 marks)B. A university parking garage needs a program, using JOptionPane only for input/output, to process a batch of vehicles exiting on the same day and calculate the total fees owed. The program must use clear separation of concerns; each task below must be its own method. No collection classes (e.g. ArrayList) are allowed anywhere.

i.    Prompt for the number of exiting vehicles, V. Then, using a loop, fill two parallel arrays of length V:

•  the number of hours each vehicle was parked (an integer per vehicle). A value <= 0 is invalid; use a nested control statement to keep re-prompting until a valid value is entered.

•  the permit type for each vehicle (a String per vehicle, either "Staff" or "Visitor").

ii.   Create a method that takes in one vehicle's hours parked and permit type, and computes one vehicle's fee using nested if-else logic (the rules below must be nested together, not checked as separate independent conditions):

•  Staff: first 2 hours free; each additional hour costs 1.00; capped at a maximum of 10.00/day.

•  Visitor: no free period; first 3 hours cost a flat 6.00; each hour beyond 3 costs 2.50; capped at a maximum of 25.00/day.

•  Any permit type that is not exactly "Staff" must be treated as "Visitor".

iii.  Create a method that takes in the array of hours parked, loops over the array and tallies vehicles into three categories: SHORT-STAY (1-2 hrs), STANDARD (3-6 hrs), EXTENDED (>6 hrs). Return these three counts without using any collection class.

iv.  In main(),

•  call the method from part (ii) for every vehicle across both parallel arrays to accumulate the batch's total revenue

•  call the method from part (iii) once

•  display one final JOptionPane showing the total revenue and the three category counts.

exam.answer:
Q6 b · parking fees for a batch of vehicles · 13 MARKS
  1. prompt for the number of vehicles V, then fill two parallel arrays of length V: hours parked (int per vehicle; a value <= 0 is invalid, so use a nested control statement to re-prompt until valid) and permit type (String per vehicle, "Staff" or "Visitor");
  2. a method taking one vehicle's hours and permit, computing its fee with nested if-else: Staff, first 2 hours free, each additional hour 1.00, capped at 10.00/day; Visitor, no free period, first 3 hours a flat 6.00, each hour beyond 3 costs 2.50, capped at 25.00/day; and any permit that is not exactly "Staff" is treated as Visitor;
  3. a method taking the hours array, tallying SHORT-STAY (1-2), STANDARD (3-6) and EXTENDED (>6), returning the three counts without any collection class;
  4. main(): call (ii) for every vehicle across both arrays to accumulate revenue, call (iii) once, and display one dialog with the total and the three counts.
Must memorise · Three counts, one return, no collections

Part 3 asks for three numbers back. A Java method returns one value. And ArrayList is banned.

So return an int[] of length 3.

An array is not a collection class. That distinction is the question: "collection classes (e.g. ArrayList)" means java.util's List/Set/Map family. An array is a built-in Java type, not a class you import, which is why F.10 and Module 8 exist and why the ban costs you nothing.

Document the slots in a comment ([0] short, [1] standard, [2] extended) and use them in that order. The alternative the ban is steering you away from is three separate fields or three methods walking the same array three times.

MEMORY HOOK: one return value, several numbers, no collections: that is an array.

Teach · Parallel arrays, and the invariant that keeps them honest

Two arrays are parallel when index i in one and index i in the other describe the same thing. hoursParked[3] and permitType[3] are one car.

The whole idea rests on one invariant: they are the same length and they are always written together. The loop in part 1 fills both in the same iteration, which is what keeps them aligned. Fill them in two separate loops, or continue past one but not the other, and vehicle 3's hours are paired with vehicle 4's permit. Nothing throws. Every fee is simply wrong.

In Module 6's terms this is what a class is for: a Vehicle object holding hours and permit together cannot fall out of step, because there is no "step" to fall out of. The paper asks for parallel arrays, so write parallel arrays; but knowing what they are the poor relation of is what Q4 was testing.

Code · question six, part b · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
import java.util.Scanner;public class ParkingGarage {    // Part ii: one vehicle's fee, by NESTED if-else. The permit decides the branch;    // the hours are only examined inside it.    static double feeFor(int hours, String permit) {        double fee;        if (permit.equals("Staff")) {            if (hours <= 2) {                fee = 0.0;            } else {                fee = (hours - 2) * 1.00;                if (fee > 10.00) {                    fee = 10.00;                }            }        } else {            if (hours <= 3) {                fee = 6.00;            } else {                fee = 6.00 + (hours - 3) * 2.50;                if (fee > 25.00) {                    fee = 25.00;                }            }        }        return fee;    }    // Part iii: tally the three categories. Three counts, one return value, and no    // collection class: an int[] of length 3. An array is not a collection.    // [0] SHORT-STAY (1-2), [1] STANDARD (3-6), [2] EXTENDED (>6)    static int[] tally(int[] hoursParked) {        int[] counts = new int[3];        for (int i = 0; i < hoursParked.length; i++) {            if (hoursParked[i] <= 2) {                counts[0]++;            } else if (hoursParked[i] <= 6) {                counts[1]++;            } else {                counts[2]++;            }        }        return counts;    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);        int vehicles = Integer.parseInt(in.nextLine());        // Part i: two PARALLEL arrays. Index i is one vehicle in both.        int[] hoursParked = new int[vehicles];        String[] permitType = new String[vehicles];        for (int i = 0; i < vehicles; i++) {            int hours = Integer.parseInt(in.nextLine());            while (hours <= 0) {                System.out.println("  vehicle " + i + ": " + hours                    + " is not a valid number of hours. Asking again.");                hours = Integer.parseInt(in.nextLine());            }            hoursParked[i] = hours;            permitType[i] = in.nextLine();        }        // Part iv: accumulate revenue across both arrays, then tally once.        double totalRevenue = 0;        for (int i = 0; i < vehicles; i++) {            double fee = feeFor(hoursParked[i], permitType[i]);            totalRevenue += fee;            System.out.println("Vehicle " + i + ": " + hoursParked[i] + "h, "                + permitType[i] + " -> " + fee);        }        int[] counts = tally(hoursParked);        String message = "Total revenue: " + totalRevenue                       + "\nSHORT-STAY (1-2 hrs): " + counts[0]                       + "\nSTANDARD (3-6 hrs): " + counts[1]                       + "\nEXTENDED (>6 hrs): " + counts[2];        System.out.println(message);    }}
Output  vehicle 0: 0 is not a valid number of hours. Asking again.
Vehicle 0: 2h, Staff -> 0.0
Vehicle 1: 5h, Staff -> 3.0
Vehicle 2: 15h, Staff -> 10.0
Vehicle 3: 1h, Visitor -> 6.0
Vehicle 4: 5h, Visitor -> 11.0
Vehicle 5: 12h, Guest -> 25.0
Total revenue: 55.0
SHORT-STAY (1-2 hrs): 2
STANDARD (3-6 hrs): 2
EXTENDED (>6 hrs): 2
Dry run · Every rule in the fee table, fired once
hourspermitwhich rule, and the arithmeticfee
2Stafffirst 2 hours free, and 2 is not beyond 20.00
5Staff(5 - 2) × 1.00 = 3.00, under the 10.00 cap3.00
15Staff(15 - 2) × 1.00 = 13.00, over the cap10.00
1Visitorflat 6.00 for the first 3 hours, even for 16.00
5Visitor6.00 + (5 - 3) × 2.50 = 11.0011.00
12Guestnot exactly "Staff", so Visitor: 6.00 + 9 × 2.50 = 28.50, over the cap25.00
Total revenue55.00

Every rule in the question fires exactly once in that table, which is how the test data was chosen: both free periods, both per-hour rates, both caps, and the not-Staff-means-Visitor rule. When you invent your own test data, invent it like this: one row per rule, so a single run proves the lot.

Two rows repay a second look. 1 hour as a Visitor costs 6.00: "first 3 hours cost a flat 6.00" is a flat fee, not a rate, so an hour and three hours cost the same, and a Visitor pays more than a Staff member who stayed fifteen. That is not a bug, it is the pricing the question specifies. And Guest at 12 hours is the only row testing the fallback rule; delete it from your test data and a program that crashes on unknown permits would look perfectly healthy.

Must memorise · A cap is a ceiling you apply after, not a rule you fold in

Compute the fee, then clamp it:

fee = 6.00 + (hours - 3) * 2.50;
if (fee > 25.00) { fee = 25.00; }

The temptation is to work out the hour at which the cap bites (for Visitors, 10.6 hours) and branch on that. It gives the same answers and it is a worse answer: you have hidden a magic number that no line of the question contains, and changing the rate to 3.00 silently breaks it, because the crossover moves and your constant does not.

This is the same shape as Q5 A's price floor, which is a cap from below. Both read as one line placed after the sum, and both then say plainly what the question said: capped at a maximum of 25.00/day.

MEMORY HOOK: compute, then clamp. Never solve for where the clamp starts.

exam.problem: Write your answer to the question above in your book first. It carries 3 marks, so write one clear point for every mark. Then open the model answer and mark yourself against it.
exam.answer:
Q2 a · define dynamic array initialisation, length, and the out of bounds exception · 3 MARKS

Model answer.

  1. Dynamic array initialisation. Creating the array with new and a size decided while the program runs, rather than from a literal list written in the source: int[] a = new int[n]; where n is only known at run time. Every element starts at its default (0 for int, null for objects), and the values are filled in afterwards. Contrast static initialisation, int[] a = {2, 4, 6, 8};, where the size and the values are both fixed in the source.
  2. The length property. a.length gives the number of elements. It is a field, not a method, so there are no brackets: writing a.length() is a compile error. It is final: an array's length is fixed the moment it is created and can never change. A String's length IS a method, s.length(). The examiner knows that catches people; Unit 7.2.
  3. The out-of-bounds exception. ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, thrown at run time when you use an index below 0 or at or above length. Valid indexes are 0 to length - 1, so a[a.length] always throws. It is unchecked, so the compiler will not warn you about it.

Where the marks are: "length is a field, not a method" and "indexes are 0 to length-1" are the two facts every other part of this question depends on. F.10 and Unit 8.1.

exam.answer:
Q2 b · debug copyarray · 3 MARKS
Compiler outputerror: not a statement

The errors, listed.

  1. int b; is not an array. It is a single int, and it is never given a value. System.arraycopy needs a destination array that already exists and has room: it copies into an array, it does not create one. Fix: int[] b = new int[a.length]; This is Q2 A part 1 being examined: dynamic initialisation, sized from a.length.
  2. System.arrayCopy has a capital C. The method is System.arraycopy, all lower case. Java is case sensitive, so this is not a typo the compiler forgives: it is a method that does not exist.
  3. i <= b.length is off by one. The last index is length - 1, so this reads b[4] on an array of 4 and throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. Fix: i < b.length. Q2 A part 3, being examined.
  4. i is not an increment. The third slot of the for needs i++. As written it is not even a statement, which is the error javac reports first. Without it the loop would never end.

Notice what this question is. Its three errors are its own part A, in order: dynamic initialisation, the length property, the out-of-bounds exception. Part A is not a warm-up, it is the answer key to part B.

Code · q2 b corrected · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
public class CopyArray {    public static void main(String[] args) {        int[] a = {2, 4, 6, 8};        int[] b = new int[a.length];        System.arraycopy(a, 0, b, 0, a.length);        for (int i = 0; i < b.length; i++) {            System.out.println(b[i]);        }    }}
Output2
4
6
8

System.arraycopy(a, 0, b, 0, a.length) reads: from a starting at 0, into b starting at 0, a.length elements. Source, source position, destination, destination position, count. Unit 8.3.

Q2 d · ten values, evens, odd sum, and the maximum · 7.5 MARKS

Read the verbs: find, count, display is three things, and the even method must do all three. And the maximum must be found in main with a for loop, not in a third method: the question says where to put it.

Code · q2 d, complete · VERIFIED ON THE JVM
import java.util.Scanner;public class ArrayStats {    // ii a. find, count and display the even numbers    public static void evens(int[] values) {        int count = 0;        String found = "";        for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {            if (values[i] % 2 == 0) {                count++;                found = found.equals("") ? "" + values[i] : found + ", " + values[i];            }        }        System.out.println("Even numbers: " + found);        System.out.println("How many even: " + count);    }    // ii b. sum and display the odd numbers    public static void odds(int[] values) {        int sum = 0;        for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {            if (values[i] % 2 != 0) {                sum += values[i];            }        }        System.out.println("Sum of the odd numbers: " + sum);    }    public static void main(String[] args) {        Scanner in = new Scanner(System.in);        // i. prompt for 10 values        int[] values = new int[10];        for (int i = 0; i < values.length; i++) {            values[i] = Integer.parseInt(in.nextLine());        }        evens(values);        odds(values);        // iii. a for loop in main to find and display the maximum        int max = values[0];        for (int i = 1; i < values.length; i++) {            if (values[i] > max) {                max = values[i];            }        }        System.out.println("Maximum: " + max);    }}
OutputEven numbers: 4, 12, 0, -8, 6
How many even: 5
Sum of the odd numbers: 39
Maximum: 15

Input is a Scanner here so the run can be printed. The ten values fed in were 4, 7, -3, 12, 9, 0, 15, -8, 6, 11.

Must memorise · Test for odd with != 0, never == 1

if (v % 2 != 0)   is odd. Always.

if (v % 2 == 1)   is odd only for positives, and silently wrong for negatives.

In Java, % keeps the sign of the left operand, so -3 % 2 is -1, not 1. So -3 % 2 == 1 is false and the == 1 test declares -3 even.

The test data above proves it. The odd numbers are 7, -3, 9, 15 and 11, and they sum to 39. Had the method used == 1, it would have skipped -3 and printed 42: a wrong answer, from a program that runs cleanly and looks right. That is why the ten values include a negative odd number, and why yours should too. Unit 3.6 and Unit 8.4.

MEMORY HOOK: "not even" is safe; "equals one" is not.

Teach · Priming the maximum: why not start at 0

The maximum loop starts int max = values[0]; and then runs from i = 1. The tempting alternative is int max = 0;, and it is a bug waiting for the right data.

If every value is negative, max = 0 never gets replaced and the program reports a maximum of 0, a number that is not in the array. Priming with values[0] cannot do that: the answer starts as a real element and only ever moves to another real element.

The same reasoning as Unit 8.4's minimum, and the same reasoning that makes Integer.MIN_VALUE the other correct prime. Starting at 0 is correct only if you know the data contains a non-negative number, and "I know my data" is how bugs are born.
